source.title: Stitched Value Model for Diffusion Alignment
source.authors: Hyojun Go; Hyungjin Chung; Prune Truong; Goutam Bhat; Li Mi; Zhao-Chong An; Zi-Xiang Zhao; Dominik Narnhofer; S. Belongie; Federico Tombari; Konrad Schindler

record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests whether diffusion and reward-model representations can be matched and stitched, using feature-matching loss and downstream retrieval performance. This is a different measurement of representational interchangeability from the original convergence measures.
record.gate_note: The direct results relevant to V4 are the stitching-interface analysis in Figure 6 and Appendix E.3. The paper also reports noisy-latent reward benchmarks and alignment outcomes, but those measure reward prediction or generation quality rather than representation interchangeability itself. Claims about model stitching in related work are cited background, not results of this study.
record.test_reason: This is mainly a method paper: stitching is a tool for building noisy-latent value models, and most results are alignment performance, which is T4 material. Appendix E.3 and Table 5 do report whether a frozen diffusion DiT's features can be mapped onto CLIP and other reward-model features, by a closed-form linear map plus a small residual stitch, with little loss. That is a new-setting result on V4 (diffusion backbone to pretrained reward model, noisy versus clean inputs). One caveat: Stage 2 also finetunes the reward-model suffix, so this is not a pure frozen stitch.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase covers only Appendix E.3. The paper's main conclusion is different: stitching a frozen diffusion-backbone head to a truncated pixel-space reward model, at a linearly compatible layer, with light finetuning, yields noisy-latent value models. These nearly match the clean reward models and make DPS, FK steering, DRaFT and DiffusionNFT faster and often better. In E.3, the closed-form loss screens out bad (late-block) interfaces but does not pinpoint the best one.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses linear feature matching followed by layer stitching and finetuning to transfer capability between a diffusion backbone and a reward model; it does not reproduce the original convergence studies' measurement procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Stitching outcome depends strongly on the reward-model cut: interfaces beyond early CLIP blocks have much higher feature-matching loss and sharply lower retrieval. Within j ≤ 4, retrieval is high and only weakly related to feature-matching loss.
record.problems: The direct interface analysis is for one diffusion-backbone/reward-model pair. The stitch search uses a probe set of 200 images, and the paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the interface results.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were extracted from the full noisy-latent reward benchmark tables or the downstream steering and finetuning tables: those report reward scores, generation quality, or compute rather than representation matching or interchangeability. Figure 6 contains additional layer-pair cells beyond the explicitly discussed selected interface, within-region summary, and late-block failure; these individual heatmap cells were not separately extracted.

untested.parts: No scaling or capability trend in cross-model alignment.
No image–caption alignment between separate vision and language models as they improve.
Relative representations and unpaired mapping are not tested. Only one model pair (SD3.5-M with CLIP ViT-L/14) has the layer sweep. A purely frozen linear stitch is not evaluated end to end.
No variation of similarity metrics or neighbour settings.
No analysis of alignment ceilings or their causes.

missing.what: Stitched versus clean reward-model performance at σ=0.1 for all backbones and reward models (CLIP, DFN-CLIP, HPSv2, Aesthetic), plus the VAE-stitching baseline, which shows interchangeability with diffusion features but heavy loss from VAE latents.
Full heatmap cells for j=8, 12, 16 and 22, showing the gradual-then-sharp degradation.

record.verdict_notes: The layer-sweep evidence comes from one pair with a 200-image probe set and no uncertainty estimates. The two models see different inputs (noisy latents vs clean images), so this is cross-modal-input stitching, not the same-input representation comparison in V4's original sources. The 'little loss' result is conditional on suffix finetuning.

versions.untested_parts: Whether independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, and data become more aligned as model scale or capability increases.
Whether image and caption representations from vision and language models align more as both models improve.
Whether different initialization seeds of the same architecture learn shared features or subspaces.

The study tests linear feature matching and layer stitching for selected diffusion-backbone/reward-model pairs; it does not test relative representations, stitching across a broad range of model pairs, or mapping without paired data.
Whether the same interpretable features or circuits recur across models.
Whether convergence results depend on similarity metrics, settings such as neighbour count, or in-distribution versus out-of-distribution inputs.
Whether alignment is incomplete or plateaus because of shared data or objectives rather than a common model of reality.

rows.check: Wrong value. In the Figure 6 heatmap the (i,j)=(4,1) cell is 0.025, not 0.027; 0.027 is i=8. The raw MSE has no normalising baseline, such as target variance, so the size of the loss cannot be read as 'little loss'. This is effectively a selection value.

rows.operation_detail: Compare closed-form feature-matching loss across interfaces as the reward-model cut moves beyond early blocks.
rows.value: rises by roughly an order of magnitude
rows.locator: Appendix E.3, Figure 6 and accompanying text
rows.note: The authors state that late reward-model blocks cannot be linearly reconstructed well from the diffusion features.
rows.check: Should give numbers. Loss is about 0.025–0.06 for j≤12, rises to about 0.21 at j=16 and about 0.70 at j=22. The rise is gradual up to j=12 and sharp beyond.

source_check.correct: Use partial for the broadly specified beyond-early-block condition. Figure 6 gives MSE 0.041–0.048 at j=8, 0.057–0.060 at j=12, 0.211–0.215 at j=16, and 0.694–0.719 at j=22. Retrieval remains 48.3–49.3 at j=8 and 20.6–45.3 at j=12; catastrophic failures occur at j=16/22.
source_check.problem: Absent overstates the result across the broad beyond-early condition, which includes successful and intermediate interfaces.

relationships.condition: Early CLIP blocks (j≤8) stitched from early-to-mid SD3.5-M DiT blocks, and the selected interfaces across SD3.5-M/L, FLUX and CLIP/DFN-CLIP/HPSv2/Aesthetic
relationships.reason: Stitched models reach R@1 of about 48–49.7 (r2, r3). Per Table 5 (text), at σ=0.1 they nearly match the clean reward models, e.g. 56.82 vs 57.90 MSCOCO I→T.
relationships.display_finding: Stitched models achieved Recall@1 around 48–49.7 and nearly matched clean reward models at σ=0.1, including MSCOCO image-to-text performance of 56.82 versus 57.90.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Performance depends strongly on the receiving cut (r4, r5). At j=12 R@1 is intermediate, 20.6–45.3; the 0.1–5.0 range applies to j=16/22.

relationships.reason: Success needs a nonlinear residual MLP plus finetuning of the reward-model suffix, not a frozen simple map. Per Table 5 (text), VAE-latent stitching does much worse (e.g. 42.62 vs 57.90 R@1).
relationships.display_finding: Successful stitches used a nonlinear residual MLP and finetuned reward-model suffix; VAE-latent stitching performed worse, with R@1 of 42.62 versus 57.90.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: The successful models use a nonlinear residual MLP and suffix finetuning, but the study does not establish that these are necessary through a frozen, purely linear retrieval comparison. That case is untested. The VAE comparison changes the source interface and does not establish adaptation necessity.
